title: 5 Sure-shot Ways to Destroy Your Team’s Trust
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that trust is the glue of an organization and that leaders erode it through small, repeated behaviors, often without meaning to. He uses a deliberate reverse-psychology device: a blueprint for destroying trust that the reader is meant to invert. The five behaviors are not listening, saying one thing and doing another, keeping people in the dark, micromanaging, and ignoring the human side of the team. Each is paired with the consequence it produces, such as lost psychological safety, rumor-swapping, or top performers leaving. He closes by locating trust loss in small lapses like an interrupted meeting, an ignored work anniversary, or a skipped 1-on-1. The piece is short and punchy, but its argument is coherent and actionable.
points: Listening, consistency and transparency are the baseline behaviors that preserve psychological safety; people who feel unheard stop speaking up and then stop caring.
Jain stresses that people watch what a leader does rather than what the leader says, so contradictions such as praising work-life balance and then pinging at 11 pm erode trust fast.
Withholding information does not create control; teams fill the vacuum with worst-case assumptions and rumors.
Micromanagement signals distrust and pushes top performers out the door.
Trust is lost through small, forgettable-to-the-leader actions, such as an interrupted meeting or a skipped 1-on-1, rather than through dramatic betrayals.
quotes: Trust is the glue in any organization. Lose it, and everything falls apart. And yet, leaders break trust all the time, often without meaning to.
This is the fastest way to kill psychological safety. When people feel unheard, they stop speaking up. Then they stop caring.
Inconsistency erodes trust like acid. People don’t just listen to what you say, they watch what you do.
Bonus points for using cryptic language in updates. When people don’t know what’s going on, they assume the worst.
Trust is built over time. But you can lose it over the small actions: The meeting where you interrupted, again.
Trust is the foundation of any organization, and is the glue that keeps your team together. So, what do you want to do? Lose trust, or build it? It’s your call.
